body:
The United States remains the largest opportunity for private-equity fundraising, but new research from Ocorian shows fund managers are increasingly looking beyond the U.S. as economic and geopolitical conditions complicate domestic capital raising.

Ocorian’s survey of 300 senior executives at private-equity fund managers, whose firms collectively manage $3.511 trillion, found that 55% identify the U.S. as offering the greatest fundraising growth opportunity over the next three years. Among U.S.-based managers, the figure rises to 78%. Europe excluding the U.K. was selected by 33% of respondents.

At the same time, 87% said current U.S. economic and geopolitical conditions were influencing their firms to seek more capital from non-U.S. investors. Ocorian also found that 62% of managers say fundraising has become more difficult in 2026 than in 2025, with increased due diligence and regulatory uncertainty among the main obstacles.

For investors, the result is a market with two simultaneous characteristics: the U.S. retains enormous capital-market depth, while Europe is becoming more relevant as a source of diversification and institutional capital.

The U.S. Investment Case: Five States With Different Advantages

There is no single measure that identifies the best state for every investment strategy. California offers technology and venture capital; Texas combines energy, manufacturing and financial services; New York remains a global financial center; Florida has attracted population and business migration; and Washington has technology, aerospace and trade exposure.

California: Technology, Venture Capital and Scale

California remains the largest state economy. State data cited by the governor’s office put 2025 GDP at approximately $4.25 trillion, with first-quarter 2026 output at an annualized $4.4 trillion. The state reported 3.7% annualized real GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026.

California’s investment profile is heavily concentrated in technology, venture capital, entertainment, advanced manufacturing and life sciences. The state says it attracts nearly two-thirds of U.S. venture-capital investment, although that figure is based on state-government analysis and should not be treated as a measure of overall private-equity returns.

The trade-off is reflected partly in public-sector credit metrics. S&P Global Ratings assigns California an AA- general-obligation rating with a stable outlook, below the AA+ median for the U.S. state sector. S&P has cited California’s large economic and tax base while also pointing to dependence on volatile capital-gains revenues and exposure to natural disasters.

California’s unemployment rate was 5.1% in August 2026, compared with 4.1% nationally.

Texas: Energy, Manufacturing and Financial Services

Texas offers a different investment proposition. The state government estimates its economy at about $2.9 trillion, making it comparable in size to a major national economy. Texas also reports 57 Fortune 500 headquarters and more than 3.5 million small businesses.

Texas has no state personal or corporate income tax and has developed a large financial-services presence in Dallas and other metropolitan areas. The state government says Texas has more than 1.6 million workers in professional services and corporate operations, including financial activities.

The labor market remains large: Texas recorded the biggest year-over-year increase in nonfarm payroll employment among states in August, adding about 159,400 jobs over 12 months. Its unemployment rate was 4.4%.

S&P rates Texas AAA with a stable outlook, although the agency’s state table identifies Texas as an issuer-credit rating rather than a general-obligation rating in this particular listing.

New York: Finance and Institutional Capital

New York remains structurally important to private markets because of its concentration of banks, asset managers, private-equity firms, hedge funds, insurers and institutional investors.

S&P assigns New York State’s general-obligation debt an AA+ rating with a stable outlook. In September 2026, S&P affirmed that rating on $264.15 million of Series 2026A general-obligation sustainability bonds and $53.025 million of taxable Series 2026B bonds. The agency cited the state’s financial forecasting and budget management while identifying unfunded retiree-benefit liabilities, debt and revenue concentration as constraints.

New York’s August 2026 unemployment rate was 4.3%, close to the national rate.

For private-equity investors, New York’s importance is less about low operating costs and more about proximity to capital, financial expertise and large institutional pools of money.

Florida: Population Growth, Services and Real Estate

Florida combines a large consumer economy with tourism, real estate, logistics, financial services and continued population growth.

The state’s August 2026 unemployment rate was 4.5%, and nonfarm employment was about 10.05 million, up 59,000 from a year earlier.

Florida carries an AAA stable S&P rating for its general-obligation debt.

The state’s investment profile differs sharply from California’s or New York’s. Real estate, tourism, financial services, healthcare and population-driven consumption are central to the Florida opportunity set, while hurricane exposure and insurance-market conditions remain important variables for property-related investments.

Washington: Technology, Aerospace and Fast Recent Growth

Washington recorded the fastest state real-GDP growth in the first quarter of 2026, at 4.5% annualized, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The state’s economy has major exposure to technology, aerospace, logistics and international trade. S&P assigned Washington’s general-obligation debt an AA+ stable rating in June 2026.

Washington’s unemployment rate was 4.9% in August.

For growth-oriented investors, the combination of technology exposure and recent economic growth makes Washington materially different from the lower-tax, energy-heavy Texas model.

U.S. Sovereign Credit: Still AA+ at S&P, Aa1 at Moody’s

The state-level picture sits within a U.S. sovereign credit framework that has changed over the past 15 years.

S&P’s long-term U.S. sovereign rating is AA+, with a stable outlook. S&P has cited the country’s diversified economy, monetary-policy flexibility and reserve-currency status as strengths, while identifying the federal government’s high debt burden as a constraint.

Moody’s downgraded the U.S. from Aaa to Aa1 in May 2025 and assigned a stable outlook. Moody’s cited the expected continued weakening of U.S. fiscal strength as the reason for the action.

These sovereign ratings measure government creditworthiness; they are not ratings of U.S. equities, private companies or private-equity opportunities.

Europe: Why EU Markets Are Moving Up the Fundraising Agenda

Ocorian’s research puts Europe excluding the U.K. behind the U.S. in perceived fundraising opportunity, but still at 33% among respondents.

European economic data also show a mixed but improving picture. Eurostat’s September estimate showed second-quarter 2026 GDP growth of 0.6% in the euro area and 0.7% across the EU, compared with the previous quarter. Year over year, EU GDP increased 1.4%.

Five EU markets illustrate the different investment opportunities.

Germany: Europe’s Industrial Core

Germany combines the EU’s largest industrial economy with deep capital markets, advanced manufacturing, automotive production, chemicals, machinery and engineering.

Eurostat estimated German GDP increased 0.2% in the second quarter of 2026 and 0.9% from a year earlier.

Germany’s sovereign credit quality remains at the highest level with both major agencies. S&P affirmed AAA with a stable outlook in April 2026, citing Germany’s wealthy and diversified economy, moderate government debt and strong external balance sheet.

Germany’s Finance Agency lists Moody’s at Aaa with a stable outlook, alongside S&P at AAA.

Ireland: Multinational Investment and Technology

Ireland combines EU-market access with a large multinational corporate sector concentrated in pharmaceuticals, technology, financial services and other internationally traded industries.

Its headline GDP figures require caution. The European Commission forecast a 1.2% contraction in real GDP in 2026, following 12.3% growth in 2025, largely because of the statistical effect of unusually strong pharmaceutical exports in 2025. The Commission expects 3.4% growth in 2027.

Ireland’s credit profile improved during 2026. S&P upgraded the sovereign to AA+ with a stable outlook in March, citing economic and budgetary performance, stronger fiscal buffers and declining net debt.

Moody’s subsequently upgraded Ireland to Aa2 with a positive outlook in August, citing improvements in economic and fiscal strength, debt reduction and the government’s financial assets.

Ireland therefore combines strong sovereign credit metrics with an unusually large multinational corporate sector, although investors need to adjust headline GDP analysis for the country’s multinational-heavy economy.

Luxembourg: Financial Services and Fund Infrastructure

Luxembourg is a much smaller economy than Germany, but its role in European finance is disproportionate to its population.

Eurostat data show Luxembourg accounted for €550 billion, or 16.9%, of EU foreign direct investment by immediate investing economy in the latest dataset cited by Eurostat, ahead of the Netherlands at €502 billion and Germany at €363 billion. The figures reflect the location of the immediate investor and therefore include financial structures and holding companies; they should not be interpreted as a simple ranking of operating-company investment destinations.

Luxembourg also has the highest sovereign rating from both S&P and Moody’s: AAA/Aaa, stable. The Luxembourg Treasury reported S&P’s AAA rating in July 2026 and Moody’s Aaa rating in August.

Moody’s cited the country’s flexible economy, strong state assets, regulatory framework and financial-sector supervision when confirming the rating.

For private-market investors, Luxembourg’s relevance is closely tied to fund domiciliation, financial services and cross-border investment structures.

Netherlands: Logistics, Trade and Financial Connectivity

The Netherlands combines a highly open economy, major logistics infrastructure, a deep financial sector and access to the EU’s single market.

Eurostat’s second-quarter 2026 data showed Dutch GDP increased 0.4% quarter over quarter and 1.3% year over year.

The Netherlands has also been one of the largest locations for immediate foreign investment in EU statistics. Eurostat’s latest data put the country at 15% of inward FDI positions by immediate investing economy among the 16 reporting EU countries.

The country’s sovereign rating remains AAA/Aaa with a stable outlook on S&P and Moody’s scales.

Spain: Consumer Growth, Services and Infrastructure

Spain offers a different profile from northern European financial centers. Its economy has a large domestic consumer market, tourism sector, services base and growing renewable-energy and infrastructure industries.

Eurostat reported Spanish GDP increased 0.7% in the second quarter of 2026, with year-over-year growth of 2.7%.

The labor market remains a significant variable: Spain’s unemployment rate was 10.5% in 2025, the highest among EU member states, although the rate had fallen by 0.9 percentage point from the previous year.

Spain’s Treasury lists sovereign ratings of A+ from S&P and A3 from Moody’s, both with stable outlooks.

U.S. state ratings add another layer. S&P’s May 2026 state table assigned AAA ratings to states including Florida and Texas, AA+ to New York and Washington, and AA- to California. These are public-sector credit assessments rather than corporate investment ratings.
